newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels say willing to talk despite boycott.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say willing to talk despite boycott.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's home said on Saturday they hoped talks with the government could resume -- but a gulf of mistrust still kept both sides apart.
With negotiations at an impasse, the rebels and President Alberto Fujimori both made bland statements of their wish to resume talks to end the siege, which began on Dec. 17.
But rebel charges that Fujimori's forces were building a secret tunnel to take the residence by storm while claiming to negotiate in good faith continued to poison the atmosphere.
A rebel spokeswoman said they had heard strange noises for days underneath the building in a posh Lima neighbourhood.

"We heard noises, not just for a moment but for several days. (At first) we didn't want to go public with this, we waited to find out for sure," said the guerrilla, who identified herself only as Comrade Micaela in a two-way radio interview with Reuters.
"We are not frightened by this," she added defiantly.

The rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), demanding the release from jail of hundreds of their captured comrades, broke off talks on Thursday accusing the government of planning to overrun the residence via the alleged tunnel.
But suggesting a softer line, the guerrillas said they were "evaluating" the situation and awaiting the arrival of a mediation group known as the guarantors commission.
"We hope so,"said Micaela, when asked in the radio interview about whether talks could resume.
Guerrilla second-in-command Rolly Rojas said in the same interview: "We are evaluating things and awaiting the guarantors' commission ... We're in constant evaluation."

Local radio station Radio Programas del Peru reported rebel leader Nestor Cerpa as saying, also via two-way radio, that he would probably meet on Sunday with the guarantors, but adding: "We still need to adjust some details" before renewing dialogue.
One member of the three-man commission, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, visited the besieged residence on Saturday with a folder in his hand. A Japanese doctor followed.

Fujimori said in a statement on Friday he hoped to resume talks to prevent bloodshed but that all talks were off if the rebels in any way harmed their hostages, including the president's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers and top Japanese businessmen.
Police loudspeakers blasted traditional Latin American songs early on Saturday at the besieged residence while heavy fog rolled in off the Pacific.

Micaela, one of two teenage girls among the rebels, issued the MRTA's salute to International Women's Day with a furious speech in defence of "outcast and exploited women who fight day after day with their children against (Fujimori's) brutal economic policies."
"As women, we are fighting for a just cause. We want to liberate all our comrades who are being held prisoner. We will keep resisting until the end," she said.

Fujimori, a divorced father of four, paid his own tribute to International Women's Day by speaking to a neighbourhood mothers' organisation in a shantytown. Joking and looking in good spirits, he dodged questions about the alleged tunnel.

Fujimori's popularity has recovered from the spill it took when the siege began. A poll published on Saturday in a local newspaper but taken before the talks were broken off showed Fujimori's popularity rose some in February.
Datum Internacional's survey of 402 Lima residents said Fujimori's popularity rose to 47 percent last month from 43 percent in January, newspaper El Comercio said.

The MRTA issued a statement via its "Rebel Voice" page on the Internet, denouncing the ill-health of 31 of its prisoners whose release it is seeking. "Most suffer these illnessess as a result of tortures, bad health conditions in the jails and bad diet," the statement said.
On the list were MRTA leader Victor Polay, allegedly suffering in his cell at the Callao naval base from a broken collar bone, vision problems and malnutrition.
U.S. woman Lori Berenson, who is serving a life sentence at the Yanamayo jail on Peru's windswept highland plains near Bolivia, was listed as having bronchitis and tendinitis.
